Reflections on Malcolm X and Black Feminism

Eugene Wolfenstein

Eugene Wolfenstein

Eugene Wolfenstein   Professor of Political Science, UCLA, and senior faculty member, Southern California Psychoanalytic Institute. His most recent book is Psychoanalytic-Marxism: Groundworks, and his forthcoming book is Inside/Outside Nietzsche: Psychoanalytic Explorations.

1

Angela Davis, thinking back to her undergraduate days, remarks that hearing Malcolm X speak “before an audience composed of the almost entirely white student population had a profound effect on my own political development. No one could have convinced me then that Malcolm had not come to Brandeis to give expression to my own inarticulate rage and awaken me to the possibilities of militant practice” (A. Davis, “Meditations” 42).1

Davis's temporal marker (“no one could have convinced me then”) signifies the black feminist challenges to masculinist conceptions of liberation that have emerged during the thirty or more years since Malcolm X was assassinated. But her statement also acknowledges the way in which, at a critical juncture in her own development, Malcolm spoke for her and to her. Hence her statement and, more generally, the essay from which it is drawn have a two-fold implication. On the one hand, it is necessary to rethink Malcolm's contribution to racial liberation from a black feminist perspective. On the other, it is important to avoid replacing the either/or of race with an either/or of gender. We require, that is to say, a critical and non-reductive appraisal of masculinist conceptions of emancipation—an understanding of the processes of development they facilitate as well as the ones they inhibit.

The present essay focuses on Malcolm X and is intended as a contribution to this critical project. We will begin with a brief discussion of the various perspectives from which Malcolm has been interpreted. This will help us to restore the political context and content of his theory and practice. It will also lead us to the recognition that the assertion of black manhood during the 1960s was accompanied by a distinctive derogation of black womanhood, i.e., by the stereotyping of strong black women as domineering matriarchs.

Next, we will develop an approach to understanding the devaluation of black women by joining (a) the analyses of race/gender stereotyping articulated by bell hooks (Ain't) and Patricia Hill Collins (Black) to (b) the feminist and object relational theory of gender-formation developed by Dorothy Dinnerstein, Nancy Chodorow (Reproduction; Femininities), and Jessica Benjamin (“Bonds;” Bonds; Like). Here I will argue that defining black manhood against black womanhood recapitulates the process through which sons assume a masculine identity by defining themselves against their mothers.

Paul Marcus PHD

Paul Marcus

Paul Marcus   Psychoanalyst in private practice and a member of the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis. His most recent books include two coedited anthologies, Psychoanalytic Versions of the Human Condition: Philosophies of Life and their Impact on Practice and Blacks and Jews on the Couch: Psychoanalytic Reflections on Black-Jewish Conflict. How individuals manage to psychologically, socially, and spiritually sustain themselves within an “extreme” situation is a topic with which I have been preoccupied for some time. In a previous publication (Marcus and Rosenberg, “Value”), I have described how a religious framework helped some devout Jews maintain their selfhood and humanity as they were violently assaulted in the Nazi concentration camps. Religion created a reservoir of meaning, a world of significance that nourished certain camp inmates when the outside world was assaulting both their physical existence and psychological integrity.

In contrast, this essay deals with the problem of sustaining the self in the extreme situation from the point of view of those who were less capable of surviving as “human beings” (Bettelheim, Heart 16) in the camps: the “intellectuals,” as the Auschwitz survivors Jean Améry and Primo Levi have called them. Whether this was the man of letters, the philosopher of science, the naturalist, the sociologist, the mathematician, or I would add, the psychoanalyst, these “intellectuals” were more vulnerable to the Nazi assault than the “believers,” those with strong religious, political, or moral convictions, such as Jehovah's Witnesses, practicing Catholics, devout Jews, militant Marxists, or Zionists.

As Améry writes:

One way or the other, in the decisive moments their political or religious belief was an inestimable help to them, while we skeptical and humanistic intellectuals took recourse, in vain, to our literary, philosophical, and artistic household gods. Their belief or their ideology gave them the firm foothold in the world from which they spiritually unhinged the SS state. Under conditions that defy the imagination they conducted Mass, and as Orthodox Jews they fasted on the Day of Atonement although they actually lived the entire year in a condition of raging hunger. They survived better or died with more dignity than their irreligious or intellectual comrades, who often were infinitely better educated and more practiced in exact thinking. (13)

I am a former diplomat who has been enriched and formed by the insights that came out of this group. There are very personal reasons why I was interested in joining the group, but I do not have time to go into them now. I regard my job as not to do what my colleagues at the Center do. I can understand what they say, but I cannot internalize what they do in the way that I can internalize my own experience and do what I did as a former diplomat. So my task in this group, as I see it, is to create a space in my world for what they are saying.

Now, my world is the world of power politics. My world is the world of statecraft, the world of diplomacy. That world is governed by a view of how countries and groups interact that does not fit today's reality. The power-politics model of world affairs is one that focuses on states—what governments do to each other. Essentially, it revolves around the idea that leaders amass political, military, and economic power. They pursue objectively defined interests against other states. This view doesn't leave any room for human beings. Throughout my intense involvement in the Kissinger shuttles, at Camp David with the Israelis and Palestinians, and with the Indians and Pakistanis my view was that if I didn't understand the human dimensions of those conflicts, I wouldn't be doing my job. And yet there was no concept of my job as a diplomat that included human beings.

I became acutely aware of this paradox in the middle of the Kissinger shuttles. My wife had died the day before the 1973 war started, and when I first saw Golda Meir, she took my hand on the day when the casualty figures from the Israeli war had been announced and said, “I lost a lot of people, too. I guess we feel somewhat the same way.” I said to myself at that time, “If you ever forget that these are people in pain, that these are people who have suffered great trauma—and that includes not only the victims of the Holocaust and the nation that was founded to be their refuge, but also the Palestinians who lost their homes in 1948—if you ever forget that dimension of your job, you're not doing your job.” But again, there was no place for those insights in the world that I lived in or came from. I therefore began to think about what that world that I lived in really was, and I came up with a different paradigm, a different picture of how the world works.

Paul Roazen

Paul Roazen

Paul Roazen   Professor Emeritus at York University in Toronto, now lives in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He is most recently author of Canada's King: An Essay in Political Psychology. His other books include Freud: Political and Social Thought; Freud and His Followers; Erik H. It has long seemed to me that looking back over this past century, the single most striking political event was Hitler's rise to power. Unlike others, I would emphasize the extent to which the Nazis succeeded by functioning within the context of the democratic rules of the game. Of course they took unfair advantage of political opportunities, and intimidation or violence played a part in their electoral campaigns. But according to the traditional standards of parliamentary democracy, Hitler's party received more popular support than many other democratically elected parliamentary governments. So the failure of the post-World War I Weimar regime to preclude Hitler's success remains an enduring mark against the vitality of democracy.

The German system can be seen as having self-destructed; proportional representation, which was viewed as democratically more fair than winner-take-all single-member districts, helped to promote the recognition of radical fringe parties like the Nazis. I wonder how many of us would continue to put such a premium on the ideals of free speech and minority rights in North America if we really thought there were a chance of neo-Nazism flourishing here; in France, today, Mein Kampf is still not able to be published. Toward the end of the Weimar republic it was, given the power of the Nazi right and the Communist left, impossible for a government to manage without invoking emergency power decrees which Hitler, once in office, was able to use with notorious advantage.

Hitler was proceeding to implement the objectives he had stated since the end of the First World War. Yet the enormity of the Holocaust that resulted still remains staggering, over half a century after the world learned the worst about what had happened. Recent comparative studies of genocide, which have, for instance, looked at the Armenians destroyed in the Ottoman Empire, or Stalin's assault on the kulaks, still do not match the horror of what the Nazis perpetrated (see Rosenbaum). Even when the continuation of the Holocaust toward the latter part of World War II was consuming vital German military resources, self-interest did not slow down the accelerating force of the Nazi determination to fulfill The Final Solution. That Germany, the most highly educated country in Central Europe, was responsible for the Nazis remains a permanent blot on the efficacy of nineteenth-century liberal ideas of enlightenment, progress, and rationality.

No one ignores the disrespect and justified suspicion of racism behind statements that presume to establish national psychologies and differential national characterologies. Anyone who has seriously pondered social and cultural phenomena knows that, from Wundt's Völkerpsychologie up to the present time, this field is beset with land mines, a slippery and dangerous terrain. Psychoanalysis has branded such attempts as generalizations without any value. Freud never committed such sins. Moreover, the Freudian idea of a universal unconscious, different from the Jungian collective unconscious, gives a purely epiphenomenal place to that which many hailed and raised as a culturalist banner. The term culturalist psychoanalysis borders on being an oxymoron, and the inconsequential statements it has generated are of as little interest to sociology as to the so-called Freudian science. If our purpose were to be indulgent, it would pertain to applied psychoanalysis—applied to a culture or to cultures—with a healthy dose of scepticism for anything going under that label. We know it, and we have argued the point elsewhere. It implies pulling out of the hat the rabbits we had previously put in it, or surprising ourselves with our own image after having surreptitiously introduced a mirror together with the object under study. These are the tricks of an unimaginative juggler. Psychoanalysis functions only within the discourse of the individual subject and its cognizance always falls on the differential traits of desire.

All the above was no hindrance for Lacan, who from time to time proffered loose sarcastic phrases, generally innuendos, sometimes funny but more often in bad taste, about the nature of Englishmen, Japanese, and Americans.

Everything that can be advanced in this disputable field is mere speculation, subject to revision and confirmation, to corrections coming from every single individual. Having said this, the fact remains that we approach the subject in analysis only by means of the discourse he or she utters under transference. And here, the raw material is lalangue made up of particular sayings and ways of speaking that come from the subject, but that he shares with a community and that join him to other families, cities, regions, and countries. Symbols, language, lalangue, a mother-tongue have made him man, and/or woman. This does not grant proficiency for a psychoanalysis of a collectivity, for as Lacan said, “le collectif n'est rien, que le sujet de l'individuel” (Ecrits 213). There is no reason to suppose that when the individual trait repeats itself we face the collective. Rather, it is a question of our inability to locate the difference in that which sounds and resounds the same.

With the exception of his “Analysis of a Phobia in a Five-Year-Old Boy” (1909), Freud seldom ventured into the actual practice of child psychotherapy, though he affirmed the “possibility of observing in children at first hand and in all the freshness of life the sexual impulses and wishes which we dig out so laboriously in adults from among their own débris” (Freud 6). Rosine Lefort's Lacanian case study of two young children during the early 1950s (in collaboration with her husband, Robert Lefort) is another contribution to this growing field of inquiry, though the work exhibits serious methodological gaps in its premises and conclusions.1

Lefort presents two case studies, one of a 13-month-old girl, Nadia, and the other of a two-and-a-half-year-old girl, Marie-Françoise. Both are patients at Parent de Rosan, a children's institution designed to care for very young children who either had been abandoned at birth and were awaiting adoption or foster-care placement, or were there temporarily due to serious maternal illness. Like several of the most well-known case studies of young children, including Freud's, Melanie Klein's Narrative of a Child Analysis (1961), and D.W. Winnicott's The Piggle (1977), Lefort's account makes for engrossing and, at times, suspenseful reading. However, there are several important differences between the analysands of these other accounts and Lefort's.

First, unlike Freud's “little Hans,” Winnicott's “Piggle,” or Klein's “Richard,” Lefort's analysands are both physically ill: Nadia suffers from chronic, painful ear infections necessitating minor surgeries, and her growth is noticeably retarded. Marie-Françoise presents symptoms of autism, cannot walk unassisted, has a very low developmental IQ, and possesses an eating disorder characterized by Lefort as bulimia. Second and no less significant, both are orphans: Nadia from birth, and Marie-Françoise after one month. Though Lefort makes very little of these realities (and, indeed, admits to being puzzled that Marie-Françoise, who knew her mother for a whole month, should be so much worse off than Nadia, who never knew her mother), it is clear that the benign neglect both girls suffer as a result of being placed in institutional care plays an important role.

Madness and Theory

The Lesson of Althusser

Gérard Pommier

Gérard Pommier

Gérard Pommier   Psychoanalyst practicing in Paris, where he also leads a weekly seminar. He is the author of many books on psychoanalysis, including Dune logique de la psychose (1983), L'exception feminine (1985), Le denouement d'une analyse (1987), Libido Illimited: Freud apolitique? (1990), L'ordre sexuel (1989), Du bon usage erotique de la colere (1994) [forthcoming in English translation], Naissance et renaissance de l'ecriture (1993), and most recently, Louis du neant: La melancholie d'Althusser (1998). He has also written a psychoanalytic novel, Ceci n'est pas un Pape, Inconscient et culture en Louisiane (1996).

When we consider today the work of Louis Althusser, we already have some difficulties remembering its political context. The situation has changed so much that we scarcely perceive the explosive potential of his writings, which now no longer present any interest except for thinkers and historians, the revolutionary being aware of them only as something for the distant future. This would not have been the case even in 1980, when the colonized countries had just obtained independence and a number of them had affiliated themselves with Marxism. In the countries that remained under the control of imperialism, the political situation was so precarious that military dictators were cracking down almost everywhere. In France finally the left came to power, at the price of a costly compromise. No one could have foretold the future, and in this context one understands the importance of Althusser's theses (which brought Marxism back to the forefront of revolutionary thought). Similarly, he had an enormous influence on a number of intellectuals and revolutionary clergy in South America (for example, the Brazilian bishop Leonardo Boff).

However, many of his theses were intimately connected to his madness, and, to the extent that Althusser himself underlined this origin, it is appropriate to examine not these theses themselves, but this articulation. For not only are the philosopher's points of view not invalidated by their source, their efficacy is also interrogated by this source. How does psychosis go about its business such that its ideas illuminate the obscurities of an epoch and, moreover, serve as a point of reference for action?

The Double Game of Psychosis and Neurosis in the Fictions of Each Epoch

In the first place, neurosis weaves social connections according to the necessities of religious belief (i.e., repression). Secondarily, psychosis bases its “theories” on these (religious or secularized) fictions which furnish the primary material for its constructions. A paranoiac today does not construct his delusions in the same way as, for example, Jean-Jacques Rousseau. He will have recourse to electronics and to the sophistication of modern science to give his persecution form, whereas he would have used religion not so very long ago. A delusion of melancholic self-punishment easily found a place for itself in eighteenth century mysticism (as was the case for Louise du Néant), whereas its employment is more random today, at least in peacetime, when the spirit of sacrifice is not openly required by modernity. This technical unemployment leaves the paranoiac hardly any other outlet than the asylum or cults, which regain their usefulness proportionately.

Between Rape and “Desired” Sex: Making a More Complex Difference

Laura Hengehold

Laura Hengehold

Laura Hengehold   Teaching Fellow in the Department of Philosophy at Loyola University of Chicago. She has presented and published papers exploring psychoanalytic and Foucauldian approaches to the political problem of rape, and is currently completing a dissertation on the relationship between embodiment and politicization in the work of Michel Foucault.

Feminist legal theorists have struggled to demonstrate that the category “rape” may include sexual acts between acquaintances or spouses, as well as acts involving little or no violence, only the threat of economic or physical coercion.1 Yet scholars are just as troubled by the difficulty of finding a common denominator among these offenses as women struggling to evaluate the justice or injustice of their sexual experiences. As Linda Bourque observes, “definitions of rape are more diverse than is generally acknowledged,” and even women “vary in the extent to which they define sexually demeaning or assaultive behavior as criminal” (285-286). Although both radical feminists and psychoanalytic theorists challenge the simplicity of the consent criterion for distinguishing between rape and “desired” sex, one wonders how the very possibility of drawing such a distinction functions as an obscure (if necessary) object of feminist desire.

The following paper seeks to understand how the difficulty of “making this difference” contributes to the trauma of sexual coercion in its own right. I suggest that the Lacanian distinction between desire and demand helps to explain how the presumption of indifference to possible sexual objects can damage women as much as the physical violence involved in many rapes. However, the legal procedures through which women attempt to reassert the particularity or specificity of their desire in the aftermath of an assault may not be able to “demonstrate” this specificity any better than other cultural rites, because the law can only represent citizens insofar as they are subjects of an undifferentiated demand. If the goal of antirape theory and practice is not to defend women's desire through a rigid legal shell but to make it possible for women to affirm their sexuality even in the absence of any demonstrable “right,” it seems important to understand how the psychological dynamics of rape transcend categories which can be represented or punished by law.

“I'm German, and I'll kick your ass!”

Turning around from the chalk-board, I found Mark—seventeen years old, six-foot-one and fairly well-built—standing across a table from Sam, glaring at him.

“Try it!” replied Sam, a nice lad, but not one to back down from machismo.

As Mark started around the table, I got in between them, put my hand on Mark's chest, and asked him what was up.

“My dad's German, and people are always saying he's a Nazi!” A slight quiver crept into Mark's voice. This surprised me, for Mark presented himself as one of the most confident bullies in the school.

“I was just saying…,” began Sam unhelpfully, reminding Mark why he had stood up in the first place.

Quickly silencing Sam, I concentrated on Mark, taking him aside and eventually escorting him out of the room to settle down.

If you have ever worked at a high school, you will recognize this as an intense but fairly typical illustration of classroom aggression. It was brief and emotional, flaring up unexpectedly and burning out almost as quickly. At the time, I was working in the San Francisco Bay Area, at an alternative high school established for students who had slipped through the cracks in more traditional educational environments. The students often identified themselves as outcasts or rebels, and they sometimes manifested severe emotional swings in the course of a school day. This experience placed me in a variety of aggressive situations, ranging from frequent verbal criticisms—expressions of the high level of underlying tension in some students—to rare physical fights. My dexterity in responding to those situations depended on many factors, including my ability to predict and understand them. In this case, I clearly could have responded more helpfully; but I had not foreseen the sudden aggression and only wanted to defuse the situation.

When I moved across the country and began teaching undergraduates at a university in central New York, I expected the level of classroom aggression to be substantively different; surprisingly, though, I did not find that to be the case. Although the aggression manifested itself in different ways (due primarily to the different socializations of the students involved), I did not find the general aggressivity level significantly reduced. In fact, I have noticed very similar concerns, coping mechanisms, and patterns of behavior in several educational settings—including private prep schools, alternative high schools, and universities. I believe that despite diverse manifestations in the classroom, most teachers encounter aggressive situations that share important origins.

Lucas Bridges, the famous first colonist of Tierra del Fuego, author of Uttermost Part of the Earth, tells, in that memoir, of finding among his possessions a “wonder worker,” a cake of Pears' soap with the power to work miracles. It is significant that such a finding should occur at the southernmost part of South America, among the world's purportedly most primitive peoples, on an island already—in the late 1890s—synonymous with the word “elsewhere.” As such, Tierra del Fuego is perfectly sited to allow an early representative of European colonialism to coin fantastic anecdotes about the local meeting of civilization and primitivism, and to send them back to the metropolitan centres of Europe. For it is in this anecdotal realm, and through the eyes of these Indians, that Bridges discovers his “wonder worker…, a certain magic soap, the miraculous effects of which the manufacturers have been too modest to claim themselves” (Bridges 219). When it comes to claims about the miraculous effects of the white man's commodity, Indians at the uttermost part of the Earth feel no such modesty—or so Bridges tells us in the anecdote that follows.

A Fuegian Indian living on Bridges' coastal property had been away some time, and in his absence his wife gave birth to a boy with remarkably fair skin and blue eyes. Bridges, whose parents were English missionaries, hastens to add that his own eyes are brown. When the Fuegian father returned to see his child for the first time, his wife told him of the “incredible transformation” which occurred when she washed the child, initially quite dark, with a cake of Pears' soap given her by Bridges' sister (220). This led to even more deception, this time on the part of the colonist, who writes:

The Proud father was so impressed by these wonders that he came seeking another cake of soap. Suspecting that he wanted to try its effects on himself and might be foolish enough to doubt his wife's story if the experiment failed, I hastened to tell him that the particular cake of soap given to his wife by my sister must have possessed some special virtue not to be found in any other tablet. He went away disappointed, but satisfied. (220)

Raul Moncayo

Raul Moncayo

Raul Moncayo   Was born in Chile and received psychoanalytic training in Buenos Aires. He obtained a PhD in Social-Clinical Psychology at the Wright Institute in the tradition of the Frankfurt School. He is currently an advanced candidate with clinical practice at the Lacanian School of Psychoanalysis in Berkeley; Clinical and Training Director of Mission Mental Health, San Francisco; Professor at the California School of Professional Psychology; and Practice Leader at the Berkeley Zen Center. It is well known that since the eighteenth century the most optimistic proponents of the Enlightenment and the scientific paradigm have been predicting the demise of spirituality. This has proven to be only partially true. Statistical studies (Wuthnow) have shown that the scientific mind-set has succeeded in establishing itself as an alternative paradigm in the thinking of most people. However, people also tend to mix scientific and spiritual views in varying proportions. Thus, science has succeeded, but on the other hand empirical evidence points largely to the survival of spirituality in the post-secular era.

Spirituality has become a growing focus of interest in contemporary Western culture. After a couple of centuries witnessing the rapid growth of science and modernity, it now is plausible to assume that postmodern-world people are interested in legitimizing and reappropriating the truths embedded in traditional cross-cultural ways and practices. Sociological studies (Roof & Roazen) describe how European and United States disenchantment with traditional Western religion has led to a search for spiritual alternatives such as Westernized versions of Hinduism and Buddhism. Moreover, it is interesting to note that, with the exception of fundamentalists, most people appear to be retaining the values of a modern secular society as well.

Political developments initiated by the Enlightenment have also helped to make the contemporary landscape possible. It can be argued that the democratic pluralism emerging from the Enlightenment not only undermined the dominant position of the Judeo-Christian religious tradition but unwittingly also curtailed the possible ideological hegemony of the scientific paradigm. The modern value of tolerance and pluralism combined with migration patterns associated with post-colonialism, plus the development of technologies of mass communication and transportation within a global economy, have led to a convergence of many traditional models nervously co-existing in the midst of scientific modernity.

Understanding the Roots of Mass Violence at the Millennium: Implications for Conflict Resolution at the End of the Cold War

At the turn of the last century, there was widespread expectation that the millennium would be completed in an era of peace. Instead, the twentieth century turned out to be the most violent century in history. As described by Stjepan Mestrovic, “This has been a century saturated in the blood of victims who were sacrificed for the sake of lofty, rational goals espoused by both sides of the political spectrum, from Nazism to Communism and so-called Democracy. From the Final Solution to the Gulag to Hiroshima to the Gulf War, and now the cruel war in former Yugoslavia—how long can social scientists pretend that humanity is becoming less barbaric?” (Mestrovic).

Similarly, it was widely expected that the fall of Communism and the end of the cold war would lead to an unprecedented period of peace and tranquility. This expectation, too, has been disillusioned. The end of the cold war has led not to peace but to an increase in terrorism and ethnic, racial, and nationalistic violence. According to Stephen Cohen, writing in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, “The breakup of multi-ethnic states, not the demise of communism, may be this generation's most profound event” (Cohen). Some have said that the twentieth century began and ended with Sarejevo.

To some extent one might have expected this. The widespread hopes that the end of World War II would lead to movement in the direction of a stronger world government, a federation of nations modeled after the United States, were unfulfilled. Woodrow Wilson's post World War I reliance on the concept of national self-determination did not work out any better after the Second World War. The concept of national self- determination was flawed because it never made it possible to determine how large or small a group or territory would be a nation entitled to self-determination. Wars like that in Northern Ireland foreshadowed the present situation. Even the proxy wars for the superpowers, like the Viet Nam War, involved the question of what was to be the nation which made its self-determination.

The club is a place that condenses everyday life and opens up its contradictions. Here we find distortions of reality in this enclosed space and the production of a different reality. There is concealment and display, but what is concealed is produced as effectively as what is deliberately played out. This is the scene. We are dancing in Sankeys Soap in Manchester. We are drinking water. These places are friendlier and safer than the alcohol clubs in north Manchester, where people stagger into each other before being sick in the toilets, where meeting someone's eye could mean getting beaten up, and where people are uncoordinated and angry. We are coordinated but not regimented. We aren't marching, but we move together fast.

The club is a place of simultaneous anonymity and individualization. At one and the same moment, it functions as a city site where a mass of people are brought together who do not know one another. We go to clubs with friends, and we move apart through the course of the evening and encounter each other again from time to time. We may dance in a group, but we cannot speak; communication is broken, and then we become bodies among other bodies. As with much life in the city, there are clusters of distinguishable recognizable faces amidst a crowd of people who are strangers. Here there is also contact. Some guy pushes past another, and their bodies glance against each other. One is rebounding and shouting, and the other shouts back. They mimic each other shouting for a minute or two, but if this is a conversation, it is one without words, and the facial expressions and gestures are each echoing the laughter of the other.

This is a place of speed, and of calm. Someone comments that the speed they take to keep them up with the beat is bitter, more granular, than last time. Not a smooth white powder, but crystalline, displaying the signs of something manufactured, carrying the traces of technology. Someone suggests that it contains glucose, and someone complains that it seems “artificial,” as if there were a more natural, unrefined or prerefined version. Now the rhythm is faster, and you move into it with more energy and a sense of exhaustion and exhilaration that carries you through at the end of a week into more intense physical work than you imagined possible. But this rhythm is repetitive and contains within it an hypnotic effect where time seems to slow down and the absence and presence of others is noticed but barely significant.

Those who know that Freud called psychoanalysis the “impossible profession” may not realize that he included education and government in the same category. Experienced teachers do not have to be reminded of the impossibility of their profession, but there have been surprisingly few psychoanalytic studies of the ways in which education arouses intense resistance in students and teachers. For this reason, Deborah Britzman's Lost Subjects, Contested Objects will be welcome, especially to readers of JPCS. Britzman, an associate professor of Education, Social and Political Thought, and Women's Studies at York University, and the author of Practice Makes Practice: A Critical Study of Learning to Teach, explores in her challenging new book how students and teachers confront “difficult knowledge”—that is, knowledge that arouses powerful feelings such as love and hate. As she notes in the Introduction, the “lost subjects in the title refer to the repressed psychic events of teaching and learning, which return to haunt education in the form of its contested objects: as conflicts, as disruptions, as mistakes, and as controversies” (19). These repressed psychic events are rarely acknowledged by educators, yet they nevertheless exist and demand attention. She might also have called her book “Education and Its Discontents,” in light of its emphasis on the unruly side of learning.

Britzman is interested in conceptualizing a theory of education that acknowledges the vicissitudes of love and hate in learning and that affirms the student's passionate attachment to the world. She draws on the work of Sigmund Freud, Anna Freud, D.W. Winnicott, and Michael Balint as well as contemporary theorists such as Christopher Bollas, Adam Phillips, and Jessica Benjamin. She theorizes that the central dynamic of education is interference, by which she means the teacher's need to challenge the entrenched forces that sustain social and political injustice, such as racism, anti-Semitism, sexism, homophobia, and xenophobia. She admits that, historically, educators have been suspicious of the psychoanalytic notion of the unconscious; yet without an awareness of the unconscious—including Freud's structural theory of id, ego, and superego—teachers will be unable to effect real learning and change in their students. Since the interpersonal dynamics of the classroom are a repetition of the conflicts that occur outside the classroom, it is crucial to understand the phenomena of transference and counter-transference. Though she does not quote the British philosopher Santayana, Britzman would agree with him that those who do not understand the past—in this case, the old conflicts and wounds that each of us carries around and projects onto others—are condemned to repeat it.

Jeffrey Mehlman's Genealogies of the Text: Literature, Psychoanalysis, and Politics in Modern France recapitulates not only a decade of essays, but to some extent Mehlman's considerable scholarly career. With its new introduction, previously unpublished essays, and anthologization of published ones, Genealogies not only returns to those topics Mehlman has engaged elsewhere (autobiography, history, psychoanalysis, literary politics, French anti-Semitism), it brings them into dialogue and into debate with one another.

The collection also includes substantial and important readings of such relatively minor figures as Paul Morand, Benoist-Méchin, and Charles Mauron, among many others. Mehlman's willingness to consider—indeed his insistence upon considering—minor, forgotten, even infamous authors and texts in order to enrich and agitate our sense of literary history is perhaps his work's greatest strength. More often than not, such marginalia are held to reveal an ugly truth about the more canonical element with which they are juxtaposed. In that sense, Mehlman's method, despite its psychoanalytic and New Historicist elements, represents a sort of deconstruction of “deconstruction in the age of academic respectibility,” demonstrating the necessity and internality of what, according to Mehlman, deconstructive discourse has treated as accidental and external—namely, the personal and political sins of its practicioners and intellectual forefathers.

As a sort of return to the Blanchot affair, its theorization, and its politics, Mehlman's book is a polemical but complex source of considerable contemporary significance. Mehlman frequently reminds us of his historically important role in this, “the first of several [controversies] I was to be involved in” (6). His role in “the de Man affair” was less central but no less vigilent, particulary when it came to Derrida's responses to these scandals.

The idea of turning to psychoanalysis to unearth the unconscious dynamics of legal inquiry and thought is certainly not new. For example, Jerome Frank's (1930/1963) masterpiece, Law and the Modern Mind, was a deliberate attempt to weave psychoanalytic theory into a complex and sophisticated critique of jurisprudential thinking and legal processes. The work of psychologists and social philosophers such as William James (1955) and John Dewey (1931) helped pave the way for this more pragmatic critique of legal formalism, deductive and syllogistic reasoning, and abstract analysis.

Perhaps the conceptualizations of Sigmund Freud come most readily to mind when raising questions of jurisprudential thought (notwithstanding contributions from Jung, Adler, M. Erikson, and Horney, to name just a few).

We attain an authentic attitude only when we arrive at the experience that—in a sense far from being metaphorical—we are all Jews.

—Slavoj Žižek

Auschwitz is the most real of realities.

—Jean-Francois Lyotard

It is perhaps a commonplace, today, to note the fact that even though orthodox deconstruction is no longer practiced, its central theses continue to inform contemporary conceptions of identity. The crux of these theses is the notion that identity is not something substantial, fixed, essential, universal, etc., but is, on the contrary, something discursively produced, a product of history, limited, variable, multiple. Identity is, so the saying goes, not pre-formed but performed, and it can never consolidate itself as a totality because there is within it a kernel of radical heterogeneity, a kernel of otherness that cannot be symbolized. What this means for our attempt to render transparent “who we are” is simply that such an attempt is, strictly speaking, never-ending; we are, it appears, never done with the process of making and re-making the self, of writing and re-writing our identity. This insight is the principle legacy of post-structuralist theorizing: my identity may in fact be determined by some larger totality—that is to say, some universal structure—but there is always some surplus that exceeds this very identity, a surplus that reveals the discursive (and hence finite) nature of the structure itself. What can never be made present is precisely this surplus. As Derrida puts it, “It is always something like an opening which will frustrate the structuralist project. What I can never understand, in a structure, is that by means of which it is not closed” (“'Genesis” 160). Despite, then, all of my efforts to bring my identity into the orbit of my understanding, to make it present to me as an object of knowledge, something always escapes me—and what it is that always escapes me is nothing else but the origin or cause of the structure itself.

In the past thirty or so years, the implications for social change seen to reside in this deconstructionist insight have not gone unnoticed: far from seeking to secure the existence of a transhistorical entity, any political articulation of identity must instead only be understood to designate a temporal moment of a particular subject—i.e., a “subject position”—and this moment is to be characterized not by universality and oneness, but rather by a plurality of particular and provisional determinations—e.g., race, gender, class, ethnicity, nationality, sexuality, etc.—none of which exist as pre-given essences. The positive political possibilities that stem from this theoretical advance have also, of course, not been difficult to detect. Freed from ostensibly totalizing discourses (e.g., structuralism, Marxism, psychoanalysis, etc.), marginalized voices, cultures, and ways of living—recall here Foucault's claim that “being anti-oedipal has become a life style” (xiii)—have emerged in all their particular multiplicity. This emergence has perhaps been nowhere more evident than in the academy, where the very nature of disciplinary knowledge has been demonstrated to be a contingent social production, and where, as a result, a number of heretofore silenced cultures and ways of being have been empowered to speak and to consolidate themselves as distinct, particular objects of inquiry.

We are all completely agreed that love is a form of suicide.

—Lacan, Seminar I

Love appears in The Four Fundamental Concepts in three guises: naively, though perhaps self-contentedly, in the imaginary; seductively in the symbolic; and impossibly in the real. My interpretation not only attempts to expose a coherence in Lacan's thinking about love specifically in Seminar XI, but it also enables us to comprehend, in retrospect, Lacan's ideas about the ethics of psychoanalysis in Seminar VII, The Ethics of Psychoanalysis. In Encore, in fact, Lacan urges us to read him backwards: “What is nice about what I tell you - don't you agree? - is that it's always the same thing. Not that I repeat myself, that's not the point. It's that what I said before takes on meaning afterward” (Encore 36).

In particular, the distinction between desire and Love in Seminar XI allows us to apprehend the Love in Antigone as destructive, impossible, as an absolute condition that is itself “ethical” only insofar as it gives rise to desire that one must not cede. To my knowledge, Lacan's “ethical desire” that must not be given up has not been disentangled, as it needs to be, from the overpowering, incestuous Love that Antigone feels for her brother(s), one in the place of a father. I say “as it needs to be,” since an underlying concern of this essay is what sort of value psychoanalysis could possibly have in the practical arenas of the clinic or social change were its ethics to be defined as tantamount to jouissance and the death drive, resulting in an unqualified glorification of “those who go crazy through a trance” (Ethics 323).

Love: Your Honey or Your Life

Love, while it is a passion that involves ignorance of desire, nevertheless leaves desire its whole import. When we look a bit more closely, we see the ravages wreaked by this.

—Lacan, Encore

To anyone interested in Lacan's idea of love as it emerges in The Four Fundamental Concepts, his statement that Freud's work on transference “led Freud to take the question of what is called true love…further perhaps than it had ever been taken” (Four 123) is noteworthy. Later in this same chapter, “Presence of the Analyst,” Lacan draws his own parallel between love and transference—through deception. Transference, he proposes, gives us the opportunity of depicting the fundamental structure of love, which is that in love we persuade the other that he has “what may complement us,” in an effort “to continue to misunderstand precisely what we lack” (Four 133). In resuming his discourse on the drive, now in the chapter “The Partial Drive and Its Circuit,” Lacan again relies on transference to generate thoughts on love. “Transference is what manifests in experience the enacting of the reality of the unconscious, in so far as that reality is sexuality” (Four 174). How can we be sure that “sexuality is present in action in the transference?” Lacan queries. And his answer is: “in so far as at certain moments it is manifested in the open in the form of love” (Four 174). All of this adds up to a view that Freud rejects, a view that Lacan articulates in the form of a question: “Does love represent the summit, the culminating point, the indisputable factor, that makes sexuality present for us in the here and now of the transference?” (Four 174).

Within the cultural Symbolic of a patriarchal society, what choices do women have as subjects? How can a woman oppose patriarchy when, in the phenomenon of what Jacques Lacan in his late work called the forced choice, its very structure readily coopts her opposition? Are all her oppositional choices forced choices? The famous Freudian question, “What does a woman want?” might be better put as “What is a woman to do?” If the historical abuses of women were not enough, then the pervasive double binds within which their actions are caught seem enough to drive women crazy. But is psychosis a choice or, if it is, is it not also a forced choice? We may answer these and other social and political questions in a Lacanian examination of a literary work, Susan Glaspell's “A Jury of Her Peers,” that, though it originally appeared in 1916 (as a play), in the last twenty years has attracted immense scholarly attention because of its combination of a protofeminist perspective and a madwoman whose psychosis leads to an almost archetypal act of murder-as-liberation.1

The madwoman is so common in literature that it has become almost a convention within recent feminist and earlier protofeminist narratives. As the figure of “the madwoman in the attic” attests, women writers have often turned to the literal or figurative psychotic to free themselves of the Symbolic of their times and to change it for later ones. While such figures, as Gilbert and Gubar suggest, may point to the “schizophrenia of authorship” (78), they may also represent a larger political agenda. By making the madwoman a figure of cultural dissidence, women writers have set in motion changes in the cultural Symbolic that may someday produce those different subjects desired by dissidence or rebellion or revolution. Because they deal with social life, realistic stories such as Charlotte Perkins Gilman's “The Yellow Wallpaper” and Glaspell's “Jury” attest to the social and personal problems attending women who take a dissident subject position. While Gilman and Glaspell suggest the high cost of female heroism when battling the cultural Symbolic, recent readings of their most famous stories seldom address the psychic costs or the ambiguities inherent in them. Though the protagonist of Gilman's “Yellow Wallpaper” rejects her husband and thereby rejects the confinement imposed upon her by both matrimony and nineteenth-century medicine, she nonetheless is falling ever deeper into psychosis. When Minnie Wright of Glaspell's “Jury of Her Peers” murders her husband and likewise rejects the abusive, soul-killing authority of a cruel husband who stands in for an equally cruel and abusive patriarchal “law,” she too suffers from an apparent psychosis. So what is a woman to do?

Events of the Clinton presidency can be illuminated by what Wilfred Bion called the basic assumptions of groups. The aims of a group, Bion explained, are

sometimes hindered, occasionally furthered, by emotional drives of obscure origin. A certain cohesion is given to these anomolous mental activities if it is assumed that emotionally the group acts as if it had certain basic assumptions about its aims. These basic assumptions, which appear to be fairly accurately adumbrated by three formulations, dependence, pairing, and fighting or flight, are, on further investigation, seen to displace each other, as if in response to some unexplained impulse. (Experiences 188)

Elsewhere, Bion indicates that changes from one basic assumption to another can also be brought about through intervention of the conscious “sophisticated” group. Bill Clinton's rise to the presidency was probably due in significant measure to the Clintons' ability to activate the pairing basic assumption (baP) in the American public. The pairing assumption involves a feeling of hope relating to sexuality, as well as to an expectation of an unborn messiah, in the form of a person, an idea, or a utopia, that will save the group from feelings of hatred, destructiveness, and despair.

William Jefferson Clinton was far from being the front-runner for his party's nomination when the first major scandal, his involvement with Gennifer Flowers, hit the media in 1992, complete with audiotape recordings of Clinton urging Flowers to lie about their affair. The candidacy seemed dead, but the scandal attracted major publicity, and Mr. and Mrs. Clinton appeared on 60 Minutes for their first famous interview as a pair. Hillary Clinton brilliantly assisted (orchestrated?) the establishment of a Bionian baP (basic assumption—Pairing) group that elicited great participation from the public.

The unborn messianic leader of the baP was Clinton's progressive political agenda, which gained a much wider following as a result of the scandal. The potentially career-ending scandal may therefore have actually won him the election, by enabling the Clintons to enact the pairing assumption.

A recent letter in The Australian (T. R. Curtis, September 5/6 1998) posed an interesting question:

When I read the Prophets I find much against injustice, a fair bit against irreligion, a little against sexual immorality, and nothing at all against abortion. When I read God's (self-appointed) modern spokespersons I find much against abortion, a fair bit against sexual immorality, a little against irreligion, and nothing against injustice. Has God changed his mind, or are they speaking for someone else?

The recent drama involving Clinton, Starr, and the US Congress has also raised similar questions in my mind. Here are some of my speculations on the subject.

From the perspective of a simplified psychoanalytic metaphor, a person's value system reflects his or her progress through stages of psychosexual development. The first three stages of life are the Oral Stage, the Anal Stage, and the Genital Stage.

The values of the Oral Stage are learned in the first year of life, when the most common source of distress is hunger and the desire for the mother's breast. The lesson learned is that happiness comes from putting something in your mouth, and being looked after.

The values of the Anal Stage are learned during toilet training. The lessons learned are to obey authority, to value cleanliness and whiteness, and to hold on to things until later, or save.

The values of the Genital Stage concern exploration, creativity, and sexuality, the possibility of mixing with strangers, and the value of tolerance.

A child moving through these stages of development may encounter adversity. He or she may respond by using one of a number of different defense mechanisms. Two of these are the Schizoid Reaction and Regression. The Schizoid Reaction involves splitting the perceived object into two polarized aspects and projecting all good things onto one part and all bad things onto the other. Regression involves reverting to an earlier successful stage and developing negative attitudes toward the stage that was failed.

It has become a truism among conservative thinkers to link the rise in aggressivity and violence in contemporary society to the decline of paternal authority. The fight against aggressivity is often couched in terms of fathers once again reasserting their authority and taking paternal responsibility. The gathering of the Promise Keepers in Washington is only the most recent example of this culture-wide movement. This kind of reassertion of the father's authority is not simply a spontaneous outburst of reactionary fervor, but a response to something that is happening within contemporary society. Without question, a certain kind of father has lost sway, but he has not-as the Promise Keepers no doubt suspect-left a void. A new father has emerged in his stead—a father Slavoj Žižek calls the “anal father of enjoyment.” The emergence of this new father has direct repercussions upon the state of aggressivity within contemporary society. For all the talk about aggressivity and violence rising in response to the absence of fathers (and the Father), what has been missed is the seemingly ubiquitous presence of the new anal father and its effects upon aggressivity. Norman Itzkowitz PHD

Norman Itzkowitz

Norman Itzkowitz   Historian and Professor of Near Eastern Studies at Princeton University. He served many years as Master of Princeton's Wilson College and is revered there as an expert in student-related educational and administrative matters. He is a member of the Advisory Board of the Center for the Study of Mind and Human Interaction at the University of Virginia. As has been indicated, the Center is an interdisciplinary group, a fact from which it draws its strength. In this mix of psychoanalysis, diplomacy, history, psychiatric nursing, and internal relations, what is the contribution of the psychoanalytically trained historian? I'll outline what it is I think I do under three headings with appropriate examples. It is important to know that these are not assigned tasks, for there are no assigned tasks within the group.

My contributions as a historian grow out of the situations in which we may find ourselves. And what I have to offer from my alleged expertise might be useful. My colleagues are well read in a variety of fields, and on any particular issue may know more than I do! But when making whatever statements I do about any issue I seek to stimulate an exchange of ideas more than to offer any definitive, immutable insight.

In history as in psychoanalysis there are many stools. The historian is minimally a three-legged one, with one leg firmly rooted in chronology, another in geography, and a third in what we can call biography. We know that history is also often written by the winners, while the losers slink off to create myths as they lick their wounds.

In the work of conflict resolution, what we often hear is history as it is passed through an emotional filter. It is a highly charged version of history, but one that is nevertheless firmly grasped and held on to and believed in. In these situations history is not something read for enjoyment; it is didactic. Not a hypothesis, but proof. The psychoanalytically trained historian must separate out the kernel of truth from the chaff of emotion, or vice versa, while treating both with respect, for both are evidence, and evidence is the raw material of the historian just as productions from the couch are the raw material of the analyst.

At this point, the historian and the psychoanalyst ask the same question: I have evidence, but what is it evidence of? Let me give one example of what I mean. It became increasingly obvious to the members of the Center as we pursued our work in Estonia that one bone of contention that stuck in the craw of the Estonians was the Ribbentrop-Molotov pact of August 23, 1939. Souring on the possibility of coming to an agreement with the West that would protect the USSR from Germany, the USSR entered into a non-aggression pact with Germany.

In doing the kind of work that we do, its essential that we know and work well with each other. For example, I have known a number of people at the Center, including Dr. Volkan, for almost fifteen years, and I think there are some on this panel who have known each other and worked with each other for more than three decades. An immature group going into an international situation and trying to enact Track II

101

diplomacy is going to have terrible struggles within itself just in trying to understand what's going on in the groups that they are working with. This was certainly the case in our visit to Kuwait, where the maturity of our group enhanced our ability to be effective.

The invasion and occupation of Kuwait was clearly a traumatic experience for Kuwaitis. Kuwait is a very modern society, a small society of approximately 600,000 people. It is a society interlinked by family and very close. While it is an Islamic society, it is quite cosmopolitan, probably because of its long history in trade. As a State, Kuwait dates back to before the United States, approximately 1750, the first time that Europeans put it on the map.

On August 2, as one of the Kuwaitis we spoke with said, it was like a bad dream: the Iraqis rushed over the border into Kuwait. Certainly, the distance was small, and it was made even smaller by the modern highways that they drove their tanks and armored vehicles down. In addition to brutalizing and terrorizing Kuwaiti people, Iraqi soldiers slaughtered, roasted, and ate the zoo animals, much to the horror of the Kuwaitis. To see their zoo transformed in such a way that the animals were being eaten by hungry Iraqi soldiers who had not been well-prepared for the occupation was a nightmare. We were also told by Kuwaitis that Iraqis took books from the library and burned them in order to make their coffee. One Kuwaiti called me at the University of Virginia a few years ago and asked for some basic references in Economics. These references had been there before the invasion. He had decided to do a report at the University of Kuwait, and then he realized that the journals that he required had been destroyed by Iraqis three years earlier. The experience of being a student and going to do your research and then realizing that the material is no longer there reminds me of the stories told by people whose houses burn, where they go back and pick up a book or whatever and then realize, “I lost that in the fire.” Such experiences reawaken the trauma. Indeed, the juxtaposition of war and peace was astonishing for those of us who visited Kuwait, and it makes us concerned about the possibility of a frozen trauma and its transmission to future generations.

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels   Assistant Professor of English and Associate Director of the Human Sciences Program at The George Washington University, and Associate Director and Treasurer of APCS. He is the author of Between Philosophy and Psychoanalysis: Lacan's Reconstruction of Freud and Hitchcock's Bi-Textuality: Lacan, Feminisms, and Queer Theory. To write and to teach writing in this postmodern age requires a series of techniques and concepts that counter the endless flow of meaningless signs, images, and representations that often dominate in our current social orders. By analyzing Jean Baudrillard's descriptions of postmodernity, I will develop a psychoanalytic theory of composition that works against the debilitating and nihilistic aspects of mass consumer culture. In order to fight against the reign of indifference that Baudrillard describes, we need to develop a differentiated model of subjectivity that is based on the Lacanian distinction between the real, the imaginary, and the symbolic realms of human existence.

In the first chapter of his book The Transparency of Evil, Baudrillard argues that we live in a post-liberation period, “where all goals of liberation are already behind us” (3). This argument, in part, stems from his idea that all forms of sexual, political, and economic oppression have been overcome or at least have been challenged. For Baudrillard, we live in a period that is dominated by the unlimited proliferation of economic exchanges, sexual relations, and political simulations. His position appears to be both fatalistic and celebratory through its insistence that there is nothing that we can do but replay old scenarios and modes of liberation in a state of utter indifference (4). Baudrillard's theory is thus predicated on the ideas that there is no hope for future change and that no one is really committed to change in the first place.

I believe that the first step that the composing subject must take in relation to this type of discourse is to affirm a commitment to the possibility of social liberation and transformation. This initial act requires a desire to actively participate in culture while one overcomes the subjective uncertainty underpinning the indeterminacy of the postmodern social order. In other terms, the writing subject must allow himself or herself to take “provisional stands of certainty” that combat the cultural production of uncertainty.

Jessica Miller

Jessica Miller   Clinical psychologist and a candidate at the Psychoanalytic Institute of New England, East. She practices psychoanalysis in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Last year on April Fools' Day the Northeast was deluged with heavy wet snow. For a brief time, while we all remained all indoors, the outdoors was like a gallery draped in a gorgeous white protective canopy. Alas, this pristine cloak provided no real protection, for beneath its weight many of the trees were cracking and breaking and when the snow melted, it left a ravaged landscape in its wake. Particularly hard hit were the ornamental trees, many of which were lost altogether, although even some of the grand old seemingly invincible giants also suffered serious injury. Yet, as if to reassure us that something is possible beyond loss itself, spring finally brought with it one of the most beautiful displays of flowering trees in recent memory.

No longer held captive indoors, I sat beneath one of the cherry trees spared by the winter's final wrath and sank into reverie. My thoughts meandered to George Washington, beloved ancestor, founding father of our country and erstwhile lumberjack. I thought of the folk tale which is so much a part of our nation's prehistory (that is, our metaphorical past, the symbolic backdrop structuring our psychic existence). The tale of course, is of George Washington as a young boy on the threshold of masculinity, cutting down his father's favorite cherry tree with an ax and voluntarily confessing to the crime. According to Mark Twain, the confession was along the lines of, “Father, I cannot tell a lie. I did it with my little hatchet.” These words capture the nation's ego ideal, the paragon of bravery and honesty. The story is likely an imaginary construction, but so much the better to fathom in search of dreamlike revelations. Furthermore, it is of particular relevance to psychoanalysts, concerned as we are with truth and the telling of it.

The story in its manifest form (the form, that is, in which it is routinely fed to American school children as part of their training in social relations) is not without its aesthetic and moral beauty. Stark as a screen memory, it has an austere and mythic quality. Its proffering of honesty as the highest of ideals; the figure of the courageous prodigy, and the forgiveness shown him by his father embody all-American simplicity and integrity which is undeniably appealing, especially in an age of lost innocence.

A study of concrete forms of democracy must reflect the peculiarities of each country. This is only possible if one focuses on the historical background, which has led to the formation of a certain collective identity. But such an approach always presupposes an understanding of identity formation processes and here psychoanalysis is of great importance. As Freud points out in Group Psychology and the Analysis of Ego, the relation between subject and other is of a twofold nature: the other is either an object of desire or an object of identification. Originally the subject has no “identity”; it acquires one by identifying itself with the other. This process begins very early in childhood and provides the matrix for all further identifications in maturity. In that sense, “identity” just means the “sum” of past identifications of the speaking subject, down to the present moment. In most cases, identification is a partial identification with the “peculiar feature” of a beloved or hatred and feared person (originally the parents). This partial nature indicates the symbolic element in each identification, which always has a metaphorical character: one is like the other. Thus mimesis is revealed as a consequence of identification with somebody.

But identification takes place simultaneously on more than one register: not only on the symbolic plane, mediated through signs or symbols, but also on the imaginary level, through the submission to the image of the other (see Lacan, Ecrits). This second case is more problematic, because the subject thus satisfies its narcissism—its fantasies of omnipotence and perfection—through identification with somebody who supposedly owns these properties. These fantasies thus aim to provide a strong real enjoyment. Freud gives several examples of imaginary identifications including, group formation, enamoration (falling in love), and hypnosis (Group Psychology).

Millions of people felt themselves being swept along by a tide of emotion following Diana's death—as if this were a collective process of shock, grief and mourning as much as an individual response, and as if those intertwined individual and collective feelings were always there, waiting to be released at a moment like this. They were not. But we live in a culture which is psychologically structured so that events of this kind evoke certain kinds of feelings about who we are and what our relationship with others is like, and then we feel them with such intensity that we imagine that they must be very deep, and necessarily true.

Rather than reveal some deep underlying psychological nature, however, they express the ways in which we have come to function as psychological beings—and, in particular, the way we absorb and display themes of unconscious emotions as subjects of a psychoanalytic culture. The week between the death and the funeral saw people represent themselves as psychoanalytic selves, and so it is worth reflecting on how this was accomplished so that we do not make the mistake of reading these events as simply confirming psychoanalysis as universally true. We might then also understand better what is really going on.

One of the powerful psychoanalytic motifs of that fraught week was that of a rising crescendo of feeling, and a sense that people were experiencing something overwhelming and barely comprehensible. Some of the descriptions of emotion in the gathering crowds in newspapers and on television could have been written by Freud to illustrate his account of mass psychology and the analysis of the ego.

Media descriptions of the crowds talked of their “disbelief” that it was possible that Diana was really dead, and the difficulty they would have in coming to terms with “the great loss.” Coming and “gathering together” was a way of showing that they were “a nation united in sorrow.” How can we make sense of this?

One of the ways psychoanalysis functions in this culture is by encouraging us to imagine that our most intense feelings are the “deepest,” and then to imagine that the reason they are deepest must be because they are welling up from our fundamental universal human psychological nature.

In 1963, Roland Barthes published Sur Racine, a volume that included a book and essay on Racine he had first published three years earlier. Barthes's version of the Racinian hero—a narrative function of binary linguistic structures and unconscious desires—was a rude defamiliarization of canonical French literature. At the time, Barthes was not even an agrègé; his thesis had been refused, he still had something of an outsider's status, and he was assuredly no expert on Racine. Raymond Picard, a leading Racine specialist, editor, and biographer at the Sorbonne, responded to Barthes in punishing fashion in 1965 with Nouvelle critique ou nouvelle imposture. Barthes replied in turn to Picard the following year with Critique et vérité, which frankly cast his own work as an insurrection against a literary police state in which Picard was a too-zealous officer. To Picard's reproach that Barthes' analysis was both unschooled and pseudo-scientific, Barthes answered that traditional literary history's obsession with the author and his intentions ignored the primary literary object. A true “science of literature” would focus, via linguistic models but also by making the critic an active and creative reader of texts, on the language that was the precondition of author and intentions alike. The tragic Racinian stage was itself being reproduced in the form of critical polemic, though Barthes's publishers (Seuil) risked turning the entire drama into farce in their zeal to capitalize on what François Dosse describes as the “Homeric combat” (1: 223) being played out vigorously in the Parisian press. Barthes's Criticism and Truth appeared in bookstores wrapped by a promotional band asking, “Should Barthes Be Burned?” By trumpeting the contest as a question of heresy, Seuil cleverly exploited the fact that a rather arcane intellectual development had become a cause célèbre among the general public. It also demonstrated how deeply and uniquely French the whole affair really was.

Students of literary criticism today must find it difficult to imagine how a major Western metropolis found itself absorbed by—and divided over—the interpretation of a seventeenth-century dramatist, and it is to the great credit of François Dosse's massive History of Structuralism that there is now a grand narrative explaining how it happened. This new work by Armando Silva is almost certainly the first psychoanalytic study of the family photo album. It also confirms Silva's ability to find subjects of effective academic inquiry in unusual cultural places, as shown by his two previous works, which focused on urban imaginaries and graffiti (Graffiti: una ciudad imaginada [1988] and Imaginarios urbanos [1992]). Silvas work on the family album as a cultural, visual, and narrative artifact is of particular interest to psychoanalysis, not only because of the study's numerous points of intersection with Lacan (and others) over matters of semiology, but also because of its focus on the album as a real object with a crucial role in the reproduction of the family as a historical and cultural subject. Rather than applying psychoanalytic and semiological theory to the photo album, however, Silva does his own thing in El album familiar, his study has a generative effect and a distinctly literary quality which merits consideration on its own terms. The importance of his work is bound to be felt in a number of areas, from studies of visual signification to discussions of the future of me family at the threshold of Postmodernity.

Despite its consistent focus on the family photo album, Silvas book has a scope wider than its object—or, better put, its scope continually widens outward from its object. El album familiar is really several books contained within a single extended reflection on the photo album: a history of photography; an inquiry into how visual signs achieve a signifying effect (Silva argues against the notion that the enunciation is produced only by natural language); a prophetic, and often personalized (but not overtly ideological), defense of the family in the face of contemporary social, electronic, and commercial trends which threaten its survival; a history of Colombia (and also of Western modernity itself) through representational trends in photography and the photo album; and, finally, a full-blown research analysis of actual photo albums from three distinct cultural regions of Colombia along with the Colombian immigrant community in New York City, complete with histograms, image samples, charts, and statistical conclusions. In short, there is enough here to provoke a wide range of interests, from psychoanalysis, literary theory and semiology to photography, history and social science.

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels   Received his Doctorate in Psychoanalysis from the University of Paris VIII. He is currently an Assistant Professor of English and the Associate Director of the Human Sciences at The George Washington University. He is the author of Between Philosophy and Psychoanalysis: Lacan's Reconstruction of Freud and Hitchcock's Bi-Textuality: Lacan, Feminisms, and Queer Theory. He is the Associate Director of the Association for the Psychoanalysis of Culture & Society. His most recent book, Composing Subjects: Lacan, Postmodern Psychoanalysis, and Academic Discourse, will be published in 1999 by The Other Press.

APCS has embarked on a crucial mission, but this mission risks being undermined by conflicts among different discourses and intellectual communities that define its constituency. My hypothesis is that if we can establish the logical relationship between these discources, we can help not only to reshape our own community but also to transform the current uses of psychoanalysis within diverse academic and social settings. Such transformation, moreover, will help motivate other thinkers and cultural workers to employ theoretical structures for the goal of concrete social change.

As a Contributing Editor of JPCS, I have been struck by the resistance of academic writers to address practical cultural issues. I do not know how many times I have pleaded with writers to focus on a particular social problem, only to have them move in the complete opposite direction. Why does this happen? My thesis is that this turning away from concrete experiences and conditions of human existence and focusing mainly—or even exclusively—on theories and abstract systems of knowledge is a submission to the ideology of postmodernism that runs counter to the most fundamental insights of psychoanalysis in genderal and Lacanian theory in particular.

The postmodern ideology at issue here is captured most elegantly and succinctly in Lacan's notion of the discourse of the University. Such discourse, which is growing more prominent, according to Lacan, privileges abstract symbolic systems of knowledge and effaces all aspects of subjective difference and cultural authority in favor of the pure production of symbolic modes of representation. In other words, people inside and outside of the academy find it difficult to address real concrete social issues because they live in a culture that constantly represses the real and hides the foundational matter and structures that underlie symbolic knowledges. Thus, in the age of the Internet, global capitalism, internationalized mass media, and Bill Clinton, we are constantly consuming more and more symbolic knowledge, but this knowledge does not lead to a stronger sense of cultural belief. Rather, our symbolic systems of knowledge often produce greater disbelief and cynical irony. The modernist goal of using knowledge to discover truth and certainty has been replaced by a proliferation of knowledges that de-legitimate traditional forms of epistemological authority. For example, the distribution of the Starr Report on the Internet resulted in more knowledge about the President, but the effect of this knowledge was mostly to make more people doubt the authority of both Clinton and Starr. In fact, in my many random conversations with students and people in public places, I found that the only common feeling of the majority of people regarding this document was a sense of disgust and confusion.

Theory versus Practice

One of the major challenges facing APCS in its efforts to promote work that will help solve social problems is to find the most effective ways, both organizationally and intellectually, of integrating theory with social practice. Theorists are often tempted to pursue their theoretical truths, elaborate them, and promulgate them as ends in themselves, viewing practitioners who do not share their theoretical insights or devotion as misguided, naive, or hopelessly benighted. Practitioners, on the other hand, often get so caught up in the pragmatic demands and concrete details of their practice and its empirical realities that they view theoretical reflection as an academic luxury that serves only to advance the theorists' careers, gratify their narcissism, or defend them against the frustrating, painful, and even heartbreaking realities that the practitioners have to deal with on a daily basis.

It is important for both groups to recognize that if there is a certain truth to both views, there is also a certain amount of illusion, which functions to protect fragile egos against narcissistic injury by inflating the importance of the activity of one's own group relative to that of the other group. If theorists forget that their insights are only as valuable as the differences they make possible in other people's lives, and if practitioners forget that blind practice, without the insights of theory, can be ineffective and even counterproductive, then all of us—theorists, practitioners, and everyone else—will be the worse for it.
