Introduction

Among the virtues of government, preserving and implementing justice stands out. Corruption is not only bad in itself; it also means that government unfairly favors some over others. Not only should government be fair in its own conduct toward citizens, but it is held responsible for securing justice in the lives of citizens. Thus, the tax code should provide adequate revenue for the business of government in a way that distributes the burden fairly; and, thus, criminals should be punished and rectification for the victims secured. Of course it is no simple matter to know what is a fair tax code, how much burden should fall on the wealthy, on capital gains, on wages, on interest, and so on. Nor is it a simple matter to know what action will right a wrong, even assuming that wrong can be set right. Nonetheless, the issue of justice looms large in the judgment we make about our government.

My interest here is not so much in which specific measures constitute fairness, or in the legal code appropriate for dealing with criminal acts. Rather, my interest is in the implications of connecting government to the feelings we have about justice. We tend to take the intensity of feeling provoked by matters of justice for granted. Yet, it is not obvious why justice carries the significance for us that it so often does. In saying this, I do not mean to question the appropriateness of feelings about justice. Rather, I am interested in understanding how virtually all interactions, personal and impersonal, become matters of justice, and what it is about justice that matters as much as it does.

Demanding Justice

We demand justice, and justice makes demands on us. A well known sports figure is accused of a brutal assault on his ex-wife and her lover. He is brought to trial. Family of the victims attend the trial, bearing witness to the often painful and disturbing testimony. By doing so, the family members experience at one remove the brutality of the original crime. When the accused is acquitted, the victims' family members insist that justice has not been done. They have the case retried in civil court, where he is convicted and fined.

In the field of conflict resolution, any conception of the Other as fixed or absolute dangerously lends itself to the readiness to dehumanize the Other.

On October 7, 1995, at a meeting of the Society for Psychological Anthropology in San Juan, Willy Apollon gave a talk on “Questions Posed by Psychoanalysis to Anthropology.” His premises were that for anthropology these questions were basically political, having to do with the specific and the contingent; for psychoanalysis they were basically ethical, having to do with universals, such as the ethics of being human. However, for each individual subject, that ethic of being human could only be articulated through the specificity of a given culture. Mental illness—and, we might add, its social counterparts, such as oppression and violence—is a sign that the articulation of the universal to the specificity of a culture was somewhat damaged for a given subject.

Apollon reasserted and expanded the tenor of Freud's and Lacan's discontent with our current postcolonial civilization in the following terms. The defect of language, its inability to express the real, and the demands and defect of the Other, make what Lacan calls “jouissance” (the immediate and total satisfaction of desire) impossible for the speaking being; in order to hold its members together, a society must offer some compensation for the loss of total and immediate satisfaction that we assume non-speaking animals have. The problem is two-fold: on the one hand, a society must veil as best it can the fact that its norms are arbitrary, in order to maintain its credibility; on the other, it must somehow compensate its subjects for the impossibility of ever attaining the jouissance we seek. The inability to do so creates a climate of such negativity that it results in the loss of credibility of the tenets necessary for the stability and cohesion of the society.

I'd like to tell you about the loss of credibility in a number of societies linked to each other by ideological rather than political or geographical ties—societies that though linguistically different have one language in common, that of psychoanalysis. Although the incident that first brought about the loss of credibility started in my country of origin, Brazil, it soon reached the international organization with which these societies were connected. Eventually it reached into their far past in European shores, and it still shadows their future in both their place of origin and in our own continental North and South America.

The impetus for this article, or what I would mark as its beginning in time, which is also a notion to keep in mind throughout the article, comes from a piece published in The New York Times Magazine entitled “The Thin Red Line” (Egan). The article circulated through the clinic where I work, and sparked much debate about what would be the clinical picture of someone who intentionally and painfully physically harm him or herself, why and how these activities would lead to the relief of anxiety, whether these were truly “female perversions,” as the author in the article contends, and what must be the biological components of these kinds of behaviors, since they couldn't have a solely psychological origin. The article itself is a finely crafted piece of writing, weaving together the clinical and treatment material with references to indigenous or tribal practices, the modern primitive movement, the mainstream notions of perversion, and the possible biological basis of the pleasure for those who engage in such practices, while holding to the assumption that this behavior is a contemporary form of adolescent self-loathing. It seemed to me that a Lacanian reading would provide a more comprehensive way of making sense of all of the material. What I would like to do in this presentation is to follow the trail of marks left behind that go to make up the thin red line that marks the difference between hysteria and perversion.

A Scar is Born

What results from the traumatic breaking of the skin? Simply, a scar is formed, leaving a trace of the rupture as a memento on the skin, a deformation of the surface of the body. As Freud has said, “The ego is first and foremost a bodily ego; it is not merely a surface entity, but is itself a projection of a surface [the editor's footnote continues:]…It may thus be regarded as a mental projection of the surface of the body, besides, as we have seen above, representing the superficies of the mental apparatus” (Freud, Ego). In the mirror phase, the infant quilts together the reflected image of its body, the name bequeathed to it, and the confirmation given to this by its parents, instituting this Imaginary identification as founded on the promise of an anticipated omnipotence and omniscience. In that the body of the infant is marked by the signifiers of the Other, it is not the body of physiology or biology with which the infant identifies in the mirror phase, but the social or symbolic body. This is a body marked by the signifier, cut into pieces by the words with which the maternal other has labeled it. As Lacan states, “This form is even tangibly revealed at the organic level, in the lines of ‘fragilization’ that define the anatomy of fantasy, as exhibited in the schizoid and spasmodic symptoms of hysteria” (Lacan, Ecrits). The organism of the infant, in being marked, or scarred, by the signifiers of the Other is transformed into the body, or the nascent form of the ego, with which the infant identifies as this is confirmed by the gaze of the Other. The mirror phase is an instant of seeing, the institution of a cycle of logical time. The mirror phase also provides the infant with its first solution to the problem of the Real, in that it provides the way for the infant to rise above its motor incapacity and the experience of the corps morcelé to perceive itself as whole, a méconnaissance to be sure, but even in error and lies the truth speaks.

Judith Butler's The Psychic Life of Power: Theories in Subjection is the sixth book for this prolific author whose work has established her as one of the foremost theorists of identity in the American academy. This most recent book closely follows her 1996 release, Excitable Voices, and her four previous books: Bodies that Matter (1993), Feminists Theorize the Political (ed., 1992), Gender Trouble: Feminism and the Subversion of Identity (1990), and Subjects of Desire: Hegelian Reflections in Twentieth Century France (1987).

Butler cannot be pigeon-holed as a Lacanian, but this book is certainly important reading for anyone with an interest in Lacan and his critical interlocutors, notably Michel Foucault and Louis Althusser. Here Butler provides an exegesis of the concepts and inter-texts that inform Freud's thoughts about “guilt” and “conscience” in chapters 7 and 8 of Civilization and its Discontents. Yet her explicit project is to attempt a synthesis of Foucault's notion of power and what she terms the “psyche.” Analogies between Foucault's thought and psychoanalysis are not easily established, however, as many Foucaultian and psychoanalytic commentators have made clear, and she is careful to offer a proviso that “thinking the theory of power together with a theory of the psyche … offers no promise of a grand synthesis” (3). Instead, with this book Butler simply “explore[s] the provisional perspectives from which each theory illuminates the other.”

But she is doing more than that. In examining the psychic form power takes, Butler implicitly argues that identity politics needs an understanding of the subject that can account for psychic phenomena and attachments. Secondly, she asks whether political agency “may do more that reiterate the conditions of subordination” (30). The book attempts to answer this question by interrogating the category of the subject and by offering a genealogy for it through Hegel, Nietzsche, Freud, Althusser, Foucault, and Lacan.

The synthesis of Foucault and psychoanalysis is fruitful for Butler because of what she feels psychoanalysis can add to Foucault's powerful analysis of subjection. According to Foucault, the very institutions that subordinate the subject also bring the subject into being; in other words, subjection is constitutive of the subject. She dubs this “the double aspect of subjection” (assujettissement), a doubling that the very word “subject” holds in tension, its etymology coming from sub-iectus, meaning “thrown under.” Psychoanalysis, in turn, offers insight into how subjects project and imagine themselves within a nexus of relations, which is not of interest to Foucault but clearly central to Butler's project.

Psychoanalysis has contributed to international relations since Freud, and most of the contributions have been metapsychological in nature. That is to say, they involve claims, for example, that a state or a nation represents a mother image or a father image, or claims that wars are inevitable because human beings have aggressive drives. These statements are true, of course. But psychoanalysis has had very little or no impact on practical issues involving large groups and international relations. A number of voices have asked psychoanalysts to work with other disciplines in order to help solve such problems. One of them came from Germany in the mid 1970s: A psychoanalyst, Alexander Mitscherlich, who had studied the German inability to mourn (since mourning would entail identification with Hitler). Mitscherlich asked psychoanalysts to move out of their offices and work with other disciplines.

Another voice was that of Egyptian President Anwar Sadat, who in 1977 went to Israel and gave a speech at the Knesset in which he said that seventy percent of the problems between Israel and the Arabs were psychological. He called it a wall, and he said, “This wall is made of suspicions and other psychological processes. Why don't we remove it?” Fortunately, the wall was not removed, because if you remove walls between enemy groups, you get identity confusion. The need is rather to make this wall more permeable and flexible.

But Sadat's advice was heeded, and because he was an important person, money was found to bring together a group of psychiatrists and psychoanalysts to study Sadat's recommendation. A group of psychiatrists, under the auspices of the American Psychiatric Association, went to Egypt and Israel and then brought a group of diplomats, psychiatrists and influential citizens from these countries to Austria and Switzerland for unofficial discussions. Our aim was to try to devise psychodynamic strategies in relation to practical issues and not just spout metapsychological explanations. We were also joined by former Assistant Secretary of State Harold Saunders and Joseph Montville from the Department of State.

What do we make today of Freud's arguments in Civilization and Its Discontents about the genesis and inevitability of aggression?1 How do current psychoanalytic understandings help us understand extreme aggression and cultural violence? Is there some linkage between cultural violence and aggression and masculinity? These are the questions this paper addresses. I suggest that Freud's arguments, though rhetorically and intuitively powerful, need much amendment, that we can draw upon alternative theories and clinical experience for greater understanding of extreme violence, and that there is a complex link between violence-aggression and gender. My thinking is tentative, and, like Freud's, speculative.

Psychoanalytic thinking about violence, necessarily beginning with a reconsideration of Civilization and Its Discontents, must concern itself not only with “ordinary,” normative, collective violence and aggression but also with the extremes of widespread vicious violence, often tied in some way to nationalism and its (tribal, ethnic, racial) equivalents, that we witness today and have witnessed throughout the twentieth century.2 Fifty years after the Holocaust, which still stands as the ultimate standard against which collective cruelty, brutality, killing, and torture can be assessed, we confront death squads, ethnic cleansing, and political rage expressed through torture, murder, and rape, genocidal murders of indigenous populations, and ethnocidal tribal warfare, not to mention widespread gang violence and gang wars in many parts of the urban world. At least, these are the kinds of violence and aggression that are in my preconscious as I write this paper.

The break-up of the Soviet Union gave birth, as you know, to fifteen independent states and to the dozens of expected and unexpected challenges that are usually described as post-Soviet phenomena. Understanding these phenomena requires in many cases an interdisciplinary approach, which may include applied psychoanalysis. Virtually every post-Soviet phenomenon could be a subject for several Ph.D. dissertations. However, since I have only ten minutes to speak, let me just identify some of the major post-Soviet issues in very general terms and give a brief illustration of how a psychoanalytic approach can help to understand them.

The first phenomenon to consider is the fact that the decline and fall of the Soviet Empire was so surprisingly short and relatively non-violent. Why? One of the explanations I can offer is that for many centuries, the borders of Russia were undetermined compared to those of Western Europe, where all territories were clearly divided. Russia's borders were not only very approximate, but also constantly expanding. This flexibility of borders specifically influenced national consciousness, making it, some would say, unshaped or undetermined. In addition, endless Russian space became not just an external factor but a deeply internalized feature of the Russian mind. The outstanding Russian philosopher Nicolai Berdiayev wisely pointed out that the Russian soul was wounded by the endless space of Russia. This notion well explains the typical Russian underdeveloped sense of responsibility for the country's destiny, its borders, as well as a dulled sense of threat, of which I could give you dozens of illustrations.

Another phenomenon is Russia's identity crisis. Certainly, Russians have been mourning the loss of their Empire and it is difficult to predict how long this process will last. Here I would like to mention just one peculiarity of the Russian Empire, and later the Soviet Empire, that has made the identity crisis so severe. Compared to the large European Empires, such as those of Britain or France, the Soviet Union was unique. Unlike Britain and France, which had a distinct national identity prior to and independent of their colonies, there was not a clear division between Russia as a nation and Russia as an imperial power. Both evolved simultaneously, and Russia's colonies lay not overseas but next to or within Russia's own borders. So, the question now is, “Who are we Russians?
